full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionIn conclusion, this study demonstrated that both BVDV and BRV are detectable in fecal samples from yaks and that their positivity statuses are strongly associated. BRV positivity was associated with age, season, sampling location, and BVDV infection status, whereas BVDV positivity was mainly associated with BRV status. Although no independent risk factor was identified for BVDV/BRV dual positivity, the detection of dual-positive samples indicates that mixed viral infection should not be overlooked in yak populations. These findings provide epidemiological evidence for the circulation and potential interaction of BVDV and BRV in yaks and highlight the importance of integrated surveillance and control strategies targeting multiple enteric pathogens rather than individual viral agents alone.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionYak (Bos grunniens) is a ruminant species endemic to the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and is well adapted to high-altitude conditions, including extreme cold, hypoxia, and seasonal forage scarcity (1). Yaks provide herders with essential resources such as meat, milk, hides, fuel, and draft power, and they play an important role in sustaining pastoral livelihoods, promoting regional economic development, improving living standards, and fostering ethnic unity (2). On the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, yak husbandry is largely based on grazing and mixed-group rearing, and their inter-herd movements across pastures, market trading, and seasonal transhumance are common, creating ecological and management conditions that facilitate the persistence and spread of respiratory and enteric pathogens (3, 4). As a result, despite the harsh environment, yaks are commonly affected by a range of infectious diseases caused by bacteria, viruses, and parasites (5, 6). These infections often compromise animal welfare, cause substantial economic losses, and hinder the sustainable development of the yak industry (7, 8). Therefore, to inform vaccine development and improve prevention and control strategies, it is essential to characterize the epidemiological profiles of major infectious pathogens in yaks.Bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV) is an enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus in the genus Pestivirus within the family Flaviviridea (9) that infects a wide range of even-toed ungulates, including domestic livestock such as cattle, sheep, goats, and pigs, as well as wild species such as buffalo, bison, and deer (10, 11). In cattle, BVDV infection is associated with diverse clinical outcomes, including fever, diarrhea, bloody or mucoid feces, oral and gastrointestinal mucosal lesions, reproductive failure (e.g., abortion), and other reproductive disorders, which compromise productivity and may cause mortality (12). Based on sequence variation in the 5′ untranslated region (5′-UTR), the Npro gene, and the E2 coding region, BVDV is classified into three genotypes with multiple sub-genotypes, including BVDV-1 (sub-genotypes a-x), BVDV-2 (sub-genotypes a-e), and BVDV-3 (also known as Hobi-like Pestivirus; sub-genotype a-e) (13, 14). Since BVDV was first described, its prevenance in China has risen from approximately 20% in the 1990s to about 57% in recent years, causing substantial economic losses (12). In addition, BVDV infection has been increasingly reported in yaks on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, underscoring the need for targeted prevention and control strategies (7, 8). However, available epidemiological data for BVDV in this region remain limited and, in many areas, outdated, thereby hindering vaccine development and the implementation of timely and effective prevention and control measures.Bovine rotavirus (BRV), another major pathogen in the genus Rotavirus (family Reoviridae), possesses an 11-segments double-stranded RNA genome. This segmented genome facilitates genetic variation through point mutations and reassortment, promoting the emergence of novel strains and potentially enabling interspecies transmission (15). Based on antigenic typing of the outer capsid proteins VP4 and VP7, BRV is classified into five G genotypes (G1, G6, G8, G10, and G15) and three P genotypes (P1, P5, and P11). BRV primarily affects calves younger than 1 month, with the highest susceptibility in those under seven days of age. Infection, either alone or in combination with other pathogens, can cause acute diarrhea in young bovines, typically presenting as severe diarrhea within 12–24 h and high morbidity (90-100%), with an estimated fatality rate of approximately 50% (16). Affected calves are commonly accompanied by depression, anorexia, dehydration, and acidosis (17). In China, the predominant BRV genotypes are G6P1, G6P5, and G10P11, and the incidence of BRV-associated diarrhea in calves has been reported to be approximately 56% (18). Although BRV G6P1 has recently been reported in yaks in China (19), the epidemiological characteristics of BRV in yaks on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau have not been systematically investigated, which is not conducive to effective prevention and control of BRV.Hence, to investigate the epidemiological insights of BVDV and BRV in diarrheic yaks raised under a semi-grazing system on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, we collected watery fecal samples from yaks exhibiting clinical symptoms of diarrhea across seven counties in this region. The presence of BVDV and BRV was detected using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis. This study provides evidence to support the development of effective prevention and control strategies, which may help mitigate the impact of BVDV and BRV on the yak industry on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. Experimental designThis multiregional, cross-sectional survey aimed to investigate the epidemiological characteristics of BVDV and BRV infection in diarrheic yaks raised under a semi-grazing system in seven locations on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau between March 2024 and February 2025. The sampling sites included Nyingchi, Tibet Autonomous Region; Yushu Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Qinghai Province; Golog Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Qinghai Province; Derong County, Garzê Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Sichuan Province; Dege County, Garzê Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Sichuan Province; Daofu County, Garzê Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Sichuan Province; and Litang County, Garzê Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Sichuan Province (Figure 1). Fecal samples were collected from yaks exhibiting diarrhea-associated clinical signs, including watery or loose feces, dehydration, depression, and reduced appetite. Clinical status was assessed by local veterinarians or trained personnel at the time of sampling based on visible signs and information provided by herd owners. Only animals showing obvious diarrheic feces, with or without accompanying systemic signs, were included in this study. Relevant factors for each yak, including age, breed, sampling location, sampling season, and ambient temperature, was recorded for further analysis. Age was classified as adult (≥ 12 months) or calf (< 12 months). Breeds included Garzê–Aba–Jiulong yak (Jiulong), Tibetan alpine yak (Alpine), Qinghai Plateau yak (Plateau), and Garzê yak–cattle hybrid (Pien). Sampling locations included Nyingchi, Yushu, Golog, Derong, Dege, Daofu, and Litang. Sampling seasons were categorized as spring (March to May), summer (June to August), autumn (September to November), and winter (December to next year February). Ambient temperature data were obtained from local meteorological records corresponding to each sampling county during the sampling period.Figure 1Schematic diagram showing the distribution of collected fecal samples by location, age, season, and breed.Map of western China highlighting six regions, each connected to three pie charts showing age, season, and breed distributions of sampled populations. Red and blue indicate calf versus adult; seasonal chart uses red, green, purple, and blue for spring, summer, autumn, and winter; breed chart uses red for one breed and blue, purple, or green for others, with numbers and percentages labeled. Regions include Yushu, Golog, Daofu, Litang, Derong, Nyingchi, and Dege, with total sample sizes ranging from 203 to 268 individuals per location.
